title: Core ideas in philosophy
description: The big questions of knowledge, ethics, mind and justice, and who said what about them.

ideas.title: Knowledge and doubt
ideas.summary: Epistemology asks what we can know and how: by reason, by experience, or by some blend of the two.

items.q: What is the traditional three-part analysis of knowledge in philosophy?
items.a: Justified true belief

items.q: Which philosopher wrote "cogito, ergo sum" ("I think, therefore I am")?
items.a: René Descartes

items.q: In the theory of knowledge, what is the difference between rationalism and empiricism?
items.a: Rationalists ground knowledge in reason; empiricists ground it in sense experience

items.q: In philosophy, what is a priori knowledge?
items.a: Knowledge that does not depend on experience, such as mathematics and logic

items.q: Which Scottish philosopher posed the problem of induction: that past experience cannot prove the future will resemble the past?
items.a: David Hume

ideas.title: Three theories of right action
ideas.summary: Ethical theories differ on what makes an act right: its results, its conformity to duty, or the character it expresses.

items.q: According to utilitarianism, what makes an action right?
items.a: It produces the greatest happiness, or well-being, for the greatest number

items.q: Which two English philosophers are the classic founders of utilitarianism?
items.a: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill

items.q: What does Kant's categorical imperative command, in its universal-law form?
items.a: Act only on a maxim that you could will to become a universal law

items.q: What does virtue ethics, the approach associated with Aristotle, treat as the central question of ethics?
items.a: What kind of person to be: good character, rather than rules or outcomes

items.q: In Aristotle's ethics, what is the doctrine of the mean?
items.a: Each virtue lies between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency, as courage lies between rashness and cowardice

ideas.title: The ancient schools
ideas.summary: Socrates and Plato set the questions, and the Stoics and Epicureans turned philosophy into a way of living.

items.q: What is the Socratic method?
items.a: Testing a belief with a series of probing questions that expose its contradictions

items.q: What does Plato's allegory of the cave illustrate?
items.a: That what we ordinarily perceive is like shadows of a truer reality, which philosophy helps us to see

items.q: What did the Stoics teach about things that lie outside our control?
items.a: Accept them calmly; only our own judgments and actions are up to us

items.q: Which Roman emperor wrote the Stoic notebook known as the "Meditations"?
items.a: Marcus Aurelius

items.q: What did Epicurus hold to be the goal of life?
items.a: Pleasure, understood as tranquility and freedom from pain and fear

ideas.title: Mind, self and freedom
ideas.summary: Philosophy of mind asks how thought relates to the body, what makes a thing the same over time, and whether choice is free.

items.q: What is mind-body dualism, the view defended by Descartes?
items.a: Mind and body are two distinct kinds of substance

items.q: In the debate about free will, what is compatibilism?
items.a: The view that free will and determinism can both be true

items.q: What is the "hard problem of consciousness", as named by David Chalmers?
items.a: Explaining why physical processes in the brain are accompanied by subjective experience

items.q: Which ancient puzzle asks whether a ship is still the same ship after every one of its planks has been replaced?
items.a: The Ship of Theseus

ideas.title: Justice and the social contract
ideas.summary: Political philosophy asks what makes authority legitimate and what a just society owes its members.

items.q: In political philosophy, what is the social contract?
items.a: The idea that government's authority rests on an agreement, actual or implied, among the governed

items.q: Which philosopher, in "Leviathan" (1651), called life without government "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"?
items.a: Thomas Hobbes

items.q: Which three natural rights did John Locke say government exists to protect?
items.a: Life, liberty and property

items.q: In John Rawls's "A Theory of Justice", what is the veil of ignorance?
items.a: Choosing the rules of society without knowing what place you will hold in it

items.q: What is John Stuart Mill's harm principle?
items.a: Power may rightly be used over a person against their will only to prevent harm to others
